titre: Prevalence and correlates of cognitive impairment in a north Indian elderly population
resume: Background: Cognitive impairment, an age-related condition, is often considereda precursor to more serious diseases such as depression/dementia/Alzheimer’sdisease. Alzheimer’s disease, which is characterized by cognitive impairment,could have a devastating impact on low- and middle-income countries whosepopulations are ageing rapidly. The disease has, so far, largely remainedneglected by researchers and national health services in India. In view of thegrowing elderly population and diverse sociocultural and geographical milieu ofIndia, epidemiological data for the condition are desirable for different populations.Moreover, there is a dearth of population-based epidemiological studies oncognitive impairment in the Punjab state of India.Methods: Three thousand and thirty-eight consenting elderly adults aged over60 years, of both sexes, residing in Ludhiana, Punjab state, India were examinedfor cognitive functioning, using a modified Hindi Mental State Examination, and ascore of ≤25 was considered to be indicative of cognitive impairment. Data analysisincluded calculations of proportions; odds ratio and their 95% confidence intervals(CIs) were also calculated. The chi-square test and multiple logistic regressionmodel were used to determine the association of cognitive impairment with varioussociodemographic parameters.Results: The prevalence of cognitive impairment in the study population was 8.8%(95% CI = 8.06 to 9.54). Increasing age, unmarried/widowed status, illiteracy,unemployment and poverty were found to be independently associated withcognitive impairment.Conclusions: The prevalence of cognitive impairment in this north Indianpopulation of elderly individuals is higher than that found in northern India. Withemerging focus on geriatric health services, cognitive impairment, which is aprecursor of Alzheimer’s disease/dementias, needs to be included in priority carewithin the national primary health-care framework.

titre: Accounting for inequality in dementia prevention programmes
resume: Growing evidence indicates that dementia risk is strongly shaped by social and structural determinants, yet prevention strategies have largely focused on individual behaviours, raising concerns about their effectiveness and equity. This perspective article examines the role of social and health inequalities in dementia prevention and argues for a shift towards multilevel, population-based approaches that address underlying structural factors, highlighting the paradox whereby behaviour-focused interventions may inadvertently widen health inequalities. The analysis describes how socioeconomic conditions, education, environmental exposures and life-course disadvantages contribute to dementia risk through the accumulation of risk across the life course, often limiting the capacity of disadvantaged populations to benefit from behaviour-focused interventions. It reviews evidence showing that structural factors such as income inequality, air pollution and early-life poverty influence brain health and ageing trajectories, and highlights the potential of population-level interventions to reduce both risk and health-care costs. The article outlines policy and research priorities, including integrating structural interventions into existing prevention frameworks, strengthening evidence in low- and middle-income countries and promoting multisectoral actions that improve physical, social and economic environments. Intended for policy-makers, researchers and public health stakeholders, it emphasizes a rights-based, equity-oriented approach to dementia prevention to achieve more effective and inclusive health outcomes across populations.

titre: Projects to support people with dementia, Shanghai, China
resume: Rapid population ageing in China is placing increasing pressure on health systems, social services and families, particularly in the provision of care for people living with dementia. This “Lessons from the field” article describes the implementation and scale-up of dementia-friendly community projects in Shanghai, a publicly funded, community-based model aligned with the WHO Global action plan on the public health response to dementia 2017–2025, designed to enhance support for older adults with cognitive impairment and their caregivers. The article outlines the design and governance of the initiative launched in 2019, which integrates nonpharmacological, psychosocial interventions such as cognitive training, social engagement and culturally adapted activities delivered through local agencies. It reviews implementation processes, including funding mechanisms, evaluation frameworks and partnerships, as well as participant feedback collected across multiple projects. By 2023, the initiative had expanded citywide, with high levels of reported satisfaction and perceived usefulness among participants, while identifying variability in implementation quality and limitations in evaluation practices. The analysis highlights key lessons, including the importance of culturally relevant, person-centred approaches, the role of sustained public financing and the need for stronger collaboration with academic institutions to support evidence-based practice. Intended for policy-makers and public health practitioners, it underscores the value of standardized protocols and robust evaluation systems to ensure quality, scalability and sustainability of community-based dementia care.

titre: Transitioning health data systems from International Classification of Diseases 10 to classification 11 in Lebanon
resume: Background: Transitioning from the International Classification of Diseases 10 (ICD-10) to 11 (ICD-11) will enhance the accuracy of health data reporting at the national level, however, certain challenges affect the outcome of such change. Aim: To document the experience of Lebanon in transitioning its mortality data from ICD-10 to ICD-11. Methods: We collected hospital mortality data from the Ministry of Public Health of Lebanon for 2022 and analysed them based on ICD-10 and ICD-11. We mapped and compared the reported ICD-10 and ICD-11 causes of death using the Analysing Mortality and Causes of Death 3 (ANACoD3) tool. Results: Discrepancies between the frequencies of causes of death between ICD-10 and ICD-11 were most visible in noncommunicable diseases. Although NCDs were the leading causes of death for both systems, the difference was higher in ICD-10 (64.0%) than ICD-11 (41.29%). Seventeen of the 20 leading causes of death generally and 16 of the 20 leading causes of child deaths (0–4 year-olds) were the same for ICD-10 and ICD-11, but with different rankings. The noncommunicable/ communicable disease ratio for Lebanon was 3.4 with ICD-10 and 2.3 with ICD-11, and the usability index was higher for ICD-10 (38.4) than for ICD-11 (36.3). Conclusion: Our findings show that moving from ICD-10 to ICD-11 at the central level can be useful in enhancing the quality of cause of death coding if there is enough data at the central level and if properly monitored by an experienced coder.

titre: Public health responses to ageing in the face of demographic change
resume: Population ageing is accelerating globally, placing increasing pressure on health systems that are often ill-equipped to address the complex needs of older people, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. This news article examines emerging public health responses to demographic change, focusing on the development and implementation of the World Health Organization’s Integrated Care for Older People (ICOPE) approach as a framework for promoting healthy ageing and maintaining intrinsic capacity across physical and mental domains. The article describes how declining fertility and increasing life expectancy are driving ageing populations, alongside weakening traditional family support systems due to urbanization and migration, highlighting a mismatch between existing service delivery models and the needs of ageing populations. It outlines the limitations of health systems historically oriented towards maternal, child and infectious disease care, and emphasizes the need for integrated, person-centred approaches addressing multimorbidity and functional decline. Drawing on examples from countries including Brazil, China, India, Mexico and Kenya, it presents the adoption of ICOPE in primary care and community settings, supported by digital tools and workforce training. The discussion underscores the importance of community-based services in enabling early detection and supporting independence, while also identifying persistent barriers such as limited resources, referral gaps and social isolation. Intended for policy-makers and public health stakeholders, the article highlights the need for sustained investment to align health systems with evolving demographic realities.

resume: The Global status report on neurology presents the first comprehensive global assessment of the public health response to neurological disorders under the Intersectoral global action plan on epilepsy and other neurological disorders 2022–2031 (IGAP). The report covers key health system areas, including governance, financing, service delivery, workforce, access to medicines and technologies, and research and information systems. titre: Référentiel de compétences en matière d’auto-soin : volume 1 : normes mondiales en matière de compétences à l’intention des personnels de santé et d’aide à la personne pour accompagner l’auto-soin des personnes
resume: Ce document présente le volume 1 du Cadre de compétences en autosoins, qui définit des normes mondiales de compétences pour les personnels de santé et de soins afin de soutenir les individus, les familles et les communautés dans la pratique des autosoins. Il s’inscrit dans un cadre en trois volumes — comprenant également un guide des connaissances et un guide pédagogique — conçu pour renforcer l’intégration des autosoins dans les systèmes de santé et contribuer à la couverture sanitaire universelle . Le cadre décrit 10 normes de compétences organisées en six domaines principaux : soins centrés sur la personne, prise de décision, communication, collaboration, pratique fondée sur des données probantes et conduite professionnelle. Ces normes définissent les comportements clés, étayés par des connaissances, des compétences et des attitudes, que les personnels de santé doivent développer pour soutenir efficacement les interventions d’autosoins. Fondé sur les lignes directrices de l’OMS relatives aux interventions d’autosoins pour la santé et le bien-être, le document met l’accent sur des principes tels que les droits humains, la pratique éthique, l’équité de genre et les soins tout au long de la vie. Il souligne également le rôle des personnels de santé dans l’accompagnement des individus pour prendre des décisions éclairées, renforcer la littératie en santé et utiliser en toute sécurité les interventions d’autosoins, notamment l’autogestion, l’autoévaluation et la conscience de soi. Dans l’ensemble, ce cadre vise à orienter l’éducation, la pratique et les politiques en proposant une approche normalisée pour le développement d’un personnel de santé compétent, capable de soutenir des autosoins sûrs, efficaces et équitables, contribuant ainsi à l’amélioration des résultats en santé et au renforcement des systèmes de santé.

titre: Heat, air pollution and solar ultraviolet radiation: mass gathering-specific considerations and research gaps
resume: This report examines the health risks associated with heat, air pollution and solar ultraviolet (UV) radiation in the context of mass gatherings, such as sporting, cultural and religious events. It synthesizes existing guidance from the World Health Organization (WHO) and other United Nations agencies, identifies challenges specific to mass gathering settings, and highlights key research gaps to inform future policy and practice. The document outlines how environmental hazards—particularly extreme heat, poor air quality and UV exposure—can pose significant risks to attendees, workers and local populations, especially as climate change intensifies these threats. It reviews strategies for risk assessment, preparedness, surveillance, communication and response, emphasizing the need for strengthened health systems, intersectoral coordination and tailored interventions for vulnerable groups. In addition, the report integrates lessons learned from past mass gatherings and provides guidance on planning and operational measures to mitigate environmental health risks. It also identifies critical gaps in evidence and proposes a research agenda to improve understanding and management of these hazards in large-scale events. Overall, the publication aims to support governments, event organizers and public health authorities in developing evidence-based, context-specific strategies to protect health and enhance resilience during mass gatherings.

resume: The rehabilitation workforce is essential for optimizing functioning and reducing disability in diverse health settings. Globally, challenges like workforce shortages and uneven distribution hinder effective service delivery. This report evaluates the rehabilitation workforce in Armenia, focusing on seven key professions and collating data to inform policies and practices that improve workforce effectiveness. Conducted using the WHO Guide for Rehabilitation Workforce Evaluation, the assessment includes various data collection methods such as workshops and interviews. Key focus areas for improvement include workforce availability, accessibility, acceptability, and quality. Education for rehabilitation workers in Armenia is advancing, with degree programs available, but issues such as inconsistent terminology and lack of formal recognition remain. This evaluation recognizes the Government's commitment to strengthen the workforce. Detailed findings and recommendations are presented alongside collected data and methodology. By embedding rehabilitation workforce actions within the national strategy and reinforcing advocacy, Armenia can promote synergy across health disciplines, ensure efficient use of resources and build a unified vision for health workforce development – ultimately strengthening health system resilience and responsiveness to evolving population needs.

titre: Global tuberculosis report 2025

It describes the coverage and performance of key interventions, including diagnosis, treatment and preventive measures, and outlines developments in financing, universal health coverage, social protection and multisectoral action addressing underlying determinants. The report also highlights progress achieved after disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, identifies persistent gaps and emerging risks such as funding constraints, and situates findings within a structured framework of global targets and monitoring. resume: Le vieillissement rapide de la population mondiale transforme les besoins en santé et impose aux systèmes sanitaires et sociaux d’évoluer vers des approches intégrées visant à maintenir la capacité intrinsèque, l’aptitude fonctionnelle et le bien-être à un âge avancé. Cette deuxième édition du manuel présente des orientations actualisées de l’Organisation mondiale de la Santé pour la mise en œuvre de soins intégrés, centrés sur la personne, pour les personnes âgées dans le cadre des soins de santé primaires, en s’appuyant sur l’approche ICOPE et sur les enseignements tirés de son application dans divers contextes. Le manuel décrit un parcours de soins structuré en quatre étapes comprenant une évaluation de base avec interventions au niveau communautaire, une évaluation approfondie de la capacité intrinsèque et des facteurs contextuels, l’élaboration d’un plan de soins personnalisé, puis la mise en œuvre coordonnée et le suivi par des équipes pluridisciplinaires. Il précise les modalités d’identification et de prise en charge des déclins dans des domaines clés tels que la cognition, la mobilité, la nutrition, les fonctions sensorielles et la santé mentale, tout en intégrant le soutien social, l’appui aux aidants et les environnements favorables. L’accent est mis sur la continuité des soins, le rôle central des soins primaires et l’engagement des communautés. Destiné aux professionnels de santé, aux gestionnaires et aux décideurs, il vise à soutenir l’adaptation des interventions à différents contextes et à renforcer les systèmes de santé dans une perspective de couverture sanitaire universelle et de vieillissement en bonne santé.

titre: Global status report on neurology
resume: Neurological conditions are a leading cause of ill health and disability worldwide, affecting over one in three people. It assesses key health system components, including governance, financing, service delivery and workforce, access to medicines and technologies, prevention and promotion, and research and information systems. titre: Landscape analysis of the opportunities and challenges for neurotechnology in global health
resume: This report presents a landscape analysis of neurotechnology from a global health perspective, examining recent developments, opportunities and challenges associated with neuroimaging, brain–computer interfaces, neuromodulation and neurological devices. The report highlights the growing role of artificial intelligence, machine learning, robotics and wearable technologies in expanding clinical applications and improving understanding of brain function and neurological disorders. The publication also examines barriers to the translation and implementation of neurotechnology, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Key issues include limited infrastructure, workforce requirements, inequitable access to technologies and datasets, and insufficient large-scale clinical validation studies. Additional considerations include patient safety, ethical concerns, privacy and the dual-use potential of neurotechnology. The report emphasizes the importance of equitable and evidence-informed development, strengthened regulatory and ethical safeguards, enhanced data sharing, and collaborative action among researchers, policy-makers, industry and communities to support responsible and accessible neurotechnology development in global health.

Cross-cutting themes include the importance of formal governance structures, sustainable financing, leadership, capacity-building, and inclusive engagement, including people with lived experience. resume: This policy brief examines the role of technologies in promoting healthy ageing and supporting long-term care systems, particularly in low- and middle-income settings. It focuses on technologies that maintain or improve functional capacity and help older people perform activities of daily living, thereby supporting independent living and potentially delaying the need for intensive long-term care services. The brief reviews a range of assistive technologies, including products for mobility, hearing, vision, self-care, cognition, communication and home safety, as well as technologies that support ageing in place through fall detection, emergency alarms and digital communication tools. The publication discusses barriers to the adoption and effective use of these technologies, including out-of-pocket costs, inadequate infrastructure, limited training and unequal access. It also analyses the inclusion of assistive technologies within publicly funded long-term care benefits packages and highlights examples of policy implementation from selected countries. In addition, the brief explores how technologies such as telemedicine, wearable devices and digital monitoring tools may enhance the productivity of the long-term care workforce and improve care delivery. It emphasizes the need for stronger evidence on cost–effectiveness, appropriate regulation and investment strategies to support wider and equitable access to technologies that contribute to healthy ageing and independent living.

Mental disorders remain highly prevalent worldwide, affecting more than one billion people, with anxiety and depressive disorders accounting for the majority of cases. The report also highlights associated mortality, including suicide, and the substantial social and economic costs of mental health conditions . The publication analyses key dimensions of mental health using data from major global sources, including the Global Burden of Disease study, WHO Global Health Estimates and the Mental Health Atlas. It examines epidemiological patterns across age, sex and regions, the burden of disease and economic impacts, alongside persistent gaps in mental health systems, such as limited data, weak governance, underinvestment, workforce shortages and insufficient service coverage and quality. titre: Rapid diagnostic test accessibility considerations for professional use and self-tests
resume: This document provides accessibility considerations for the design, development and implementation of rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) intended for professional use and self-testing. Developed by the World Health Organization through a consultative process involving technical experts, end users and organizations representing persons with disabilities, the publication addresses barriers that may limit equitable access to diagnostic technologies. The guidance applies to a broad range of rapid diagnostics, including tests for HIV, tuberculosis, malaria, SARS-CoV-2, hepatitis, syphilis and pregnancy, among others. The publication outlines practical considerations to improve accessibility and usability across labeling, instructions for use, physical components, digital interfaces, specimen collection, result interpretation and disposal. It emphasizes principles of universal design, multimodal communication, plain language, compatibility with assistive technologies, and engagement of end users throughout product development and evaluation. The document also discusses the relevance of accessibility for WHO prequalification and post-market surveillance processes. Its objective is to support manufacturers, regulators, procurement agencies, implementing partners and donors in promoting equitable access to diagnostic testing for persons with disabilities, older adults and other populations facing barriers to health services.

resume: Este documento presenta el volumen 1 del Marco de competencias en autocuidado, que define normas mundiales de competencias para que los trabajadores de la salud y de atención apoyen a las personas, las familias y las comunidades en la práctica del autocuidado. Forma parte de un marco compuesto por tres volúmenes —que incluyen además una guía de conocimientos y una guía curricular— diseñado para fortalecer la integración del autocuidado en los sistemas de salud y contribuir a la cobertura sanitaria universal . El marco describe 10 normas de competencias organizadas en seis dominios fundamentales: atención centrada en la persona, toma de decisiones, comunicación, colaboración, práctica basada en la evidencia y conducta profesional. Estas normas especifican los comportamientos clave, sustentados en conocimientos, habilidades y actitudes, que los trabajadores de la salud deben desarrollar para apoyar eficazmente las intervenciones de autocuidado. Basado en las directrices de la OMS sobre intervenciones de autocuidado para la salud y el bienestar, el documento hace hincapié en principios como los derechos humanos, la práctica ética, la equidad de género y la atención a lo largo del curso de la vida. Asimismo, destaca el papel de los trabajadores de la salud en facilitar la toma de decisiones informadas, fortalecer la alfabetización en salud y apoyar el uso seguro de intervenciones de autocuidado, incluyendo el automanejo, la autoevaluación y la autoconciencia. En conjunto, el marco tiene como objetivo orientar la educación, la práctica y las políticas mediante un enfoque estandarizado para el desarrollo de un personal sanitario competente, capaz de apoyar un autocuidado seguro, eficaz y equitativo, mejorando así los resultados en salud y fortaleciendo los sistemas de salud.

resume: Громади відіграють вирішальну роль у запобіганні самогубствам. Цей інструментарій створений на основі звіту Всесвітньої організації охорони здоров’я (ВООЗ) «Запобігання самогубствам: глобальний імператив» (WHO, 2014) та містить практичні поради для залучення громад до діяльності із запобігання самогубствам. Залучення громад — активний колективний висхідний процес, за допомогою якого громади можуть впливати на політику і послуги та формувати їх (McLeroy et al., 2003). Для цього громади можуть розпочати втілювати важливі та відповідні місцевому контексту заходи. Однак, попри те, що техніки залучення громад все більше набувають популярності як інноваційні підходи до охорони фізичного та психічного здоров’я, часто бракує наочних прикладів та рекомендацій для їхньої успішної розробки та виконання (Mendel et al., 2011). За умови належного впровадження проєкти залучення громад можуть бути дуже ефективними у вирішенні проблем психічного здоров’я в цілому та запобігання самогубствам зокрема. Такі підходи часто є відносно маловитратними і тому особливо привабливі для країн з низьким та середнім рівнем доходу, де стигма та табу часто обмежують людям із суїцидальною поведінкою доступ до якісної допомоги. Коли мова йде про такі делікатні проблеми, як запобігання самогубствам, часто важко зрозуміти, як і з чого починати діяльність. Тому цей інструментарій містить деякі практичні поради, які можуть використовувати громади усього світу, незалежно від наявних ресурсів чи поточної ситуації із запобігання самогубствам.

titre: Dementia in refugees and migrants: epidemiology, public health implications and global responses
resume: Population ageing and increasing global migration are reshaping health needs worldwide, bringing growing attention to dementia among refugees and migrants as a complex public health concern. This Global Evidence Review on Health and Migration examines the epidemiology, determinants and care needs of dementia in these populations, aiming to inform evidence-based policies and responses. Drawing on a comprehensive scoping review of scientific and grey literature, the report analyses evidence on prevalence, risk factors, health literacy, access to health and social services, and the preparedness of systems to provide culturally appropriate diagnosis, care and support, structured in line with the action areas of the WHO Global action plan on the public health response to dementia 2017–2025. It highlights significant gaps in data, particularly in low- and middle-income countries and emergency settings, as well as challenges such as underdiagnosis, barriers to access, limited use of culturally adapted assessment tools and insufficient training of health professionals. The review also examines the experiences of carers and the inclusion of refugees and migrants in dementia policies, emphasizing the role of social determinants and migration-related factors across the care continuum. Findings underscore the need for equity-oriented, culturally sensitive approaches. Intended for policy-makers, researchers and practitioners, the report provides policy considerations to strengthen inclusive, evidence-informed responses to dementia in diverse and mobile populations.

resume: This report describes the development and initial implementation of Georgia’s first state-funded rehabilitation service package using the World Health Organization’s Package of interventions for rehabilitation (PIR). The publication details the processes used to define rehabilitation service types, estimate costs, determine eligibility criteria and prepare implementation mechanisms for outpatient and inpatient rehabilitation services. It also examines the establishment of governance structures, authorization of rehabilitation providers and planned expansion of services. In addition, the report highlights lessons learned from applying the PIR in policy development and health system strengthening, emphasizing the importance of sustainable financing, workforce development, rehabilitation data systems and integration of rehabilitation into universal health coverage.

titre: A global health strategy for 2025-2028: advancing equity and resilience in a turbulent world: fourteenth General Programme of Work
resume: This document presents the World Health Organization’s Fourteenth General Programme of Work (GPW 14) for 2025–2028, which establishes a global health strategy aimed at advancing health equity and strengthening resilience in an increasingly complex and turbulent world. Building on lessons learned from the COVID-19 pandemic, the evaluation of GPW 13 and ongoing WHO transformation efforts, the strategy outlines a common agenda for Member States, WHO and partners to accelerate progress towards the health-related Sustainable Development Goals. The publication examines the evolving global context, including climate change, demographic shifts, health inequities, humanitarian crises and emerging health threats, and analyses their implications for health systems and population well-being. The document defines WHO’s mission to promote, provide and protect health through six strategic objectives focused on climate-related health risks, determinants of health, primary health care, universal health coverage and health emergency preparedness and response. It also introduces a results framework based on joint and corporate outcomes, a theory of change for collective action and priorities for strengthening WHO’s organizational performance, financing and country-level capacities. The strategy emphasizes partnership, equity, data systems, innovation and sustainable health system transformation as central components of global health action for the period 2025–2028.

titre: WHO Operational Review of Türkiye's approach to noncommunicable diseases during the emergency response to the 2023 earthquakes
resume: The scale of destruction from the 2023 Türkiye earthquakes substantially increased health needs for the affected population, requiring a wide-ranging response from the Government of Türkiye and its partners. This NCD Operational Review, conducted by WHO and Türkiye's Ministry of Health, focuses on the response to noncommunicable diseases, which were a significant cause of morbidity and mortality prior to the emergency. The review aims to identify good practice, lessons learned and suggest actions to address NCD challenges in response efforts, while also contributing to system strengthening and resilience for future emergencies. Türkiye’s comprehensive package of health services, including chronic NCD management, and support programme for refugees, was critical to resilience. Further success factors included integrating NCD management throughout preparedness, response and recovery; well developed preparedness planning; the inclusion of NCDs in rapid assessments; contingency planning and rapid capacity-building to deliver primary care services and maintain access to essential medicines; and coordinated evacuation of patients for specialist care where required. Further work is planned to continue to strengthen health information systems, community engagement approaches, and to develop and share new guidance and tools. This review, alongside other recent NCD-focused operational reviews, provides critical lessons for the response to NCDs in emergencies.

titre: Integrated care for older people (ICOPE): guidance for person-centred assessment and pathways in primary care
resume: Population ageing is reshaping health and social care systems worldwide, requiring approaches that move beyond disease-focused models towards maintaining functional ability and well-being in older age. This second edition of the handbook presents updated guidance from the World Health Organization on delivering person-centred, integrated care for older people within primary care settings, building on the Integrated care for older people (ICOPE) framework and incorporating lessons from implementation across diverse contexts. It outlines a structured four-step care pathway encompassing basic assessment and community-level interventions, in-depth assessment, development of personalized care plans, and coordinated implementation and monitoring. The guidance describes how to identify and manage declines in intrinsic capacity across key domains such as cognition, mobility, nutrition, sensory function and mental health, while addressing social support, carers’ needs and environmental factors. Emphasis is placed on multidisciplinary teamwork, community engagement and continuity of care across health and social services. Designed as a practical tool for health workers, managers and policy-makers, the handbook supports adaptation to different health system capacities and resource settings, and aims to strengthen primary health care in line with universal health coverage and healthy ageing objectives.

titre: Integrating services for maternal, newborn and child health and noncommunicable diseases at district- level facilities: Viet Nam country perspective
resume: This country perspective analyses the burden of noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) among women in Viet Nam, including during pregnancy and the postnatal period, and examines opportunities to integrate NCD prevention and control into maternal health services at district-level and related health facilities. Using a mixed-methods approach that combined a review of national and international data sources, policies and guidelines with qualitative interviews involving policy-makers, managers and health-care providers, the report assesses the prevalence of major NCDs and risk factors, including cardiovascular diseases, cancer, diabetes, mental health conditions and chronic respiratory diseases. The document reviews the organization of maternal and NCD services, existing policies, workforce capacity, financing mechanisms, availability of medicines and equipment, and health information systems. Findings indicate a growing burden of NCDs among women and increasing exposure to associated risk factors, while highlighting progress in screening and management of selected conditions during pregnancy. At the same time, gaps remain in continuity of care, mental health services, referral pathways, monitoring systems and equitable access to services. The report identifies priority areas for strengthening the integration of NCD prevention, early detection and management within maternal health care to improve women’s health outcomes across the life course.

titre: Promoting physical activity and healthy diets for healthy ageing in the WHO European Region
resume: Lifestyle and medical advances that contribute to longevity are achievements to celebrate, but they have brought considerable and unintended social, economic and health challenges as life expectancy increases faster than life-years spent in good health. In this context, healthy ageing – defined by WHO as a process of developing and maintaining functional abilities to foster well-being in older adults – not only increases the welfare of older adults, but also directly influences health-care and long-term care costs. Although health status in older ages mainly is dependent on lifestyles determined during adulthood and youth, the level of physical activity and quality of diet in older age are also important determinants of health, well-being, functional ability, mobility and independence. For most older people, healthy ageing means much more than just the absence of diseases; it also represents the maintenance of good functional ability. This report advocates for investment in promoting healthy lifestyles in the older population to encourage active healthy ageing and increase healthy life expectancy. Inspiring examples of innovations in promoting physical activity and healthy diets from across the WHO European Region are presented to support implementation and scale-up of interventions by Member States.

titre: WHO guideline on the prevention and diagnosis of rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease
resume: This guideline provides evidence-informed recommendations for the prevention and diagnosis of rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease, conditions that remain significant causes of morbidity and mortality in low- and middle-income countries and among vulnerable populations. Rheumatic heart disease, which affected an estimated 55 million people globally in 2021, arises from untreated or recurrent group A streptococcal infections and is closely associated with socioeconomic determinants such as poverty, overcrowding and limited access to health care. The document aims to support countries in reducing disease burden through improved early detection, timely treatment and effective prevention strategies. Developed in accordance with WHO guideline methodology, the publication synthesizes current scientific evidence and expert consensus to formulate recommendations on primary and secondary prevention and selected aspects of clinical management. It addresses key areas including diagnosis and treatment of streptococcal pharyngitis and skin infections, use of echocardiography for diagnosis and screening, and antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent recurrence. The guideline places particular emphasis on populations at moderate to high risk and includes considerations for implementation, monitoring and adaptation in different settings. Intended for policy-makers, programme managers and health-care providers, it supports the development of national policies and clinical protocols to improve prevention, diagnosis and care.

resume: A cross-sectional study was conducted in specialist children's hospitals in Alexandria, which aimed to evaluate the current regimen of secondary prophylaxis for children suffering from rheumatic heart disease. titre: Therapeutic education of patients with coronary heart disease: training guide for general practitioners
resume: The guide is one of outcomes of a pilot project on the therapeutic education of patients with coronary heart disease, carried out between 1998 and 2003, in the Udine and Volterra areas, Italy. The aim of the project was to train general practitioners as trainers of groups of patients or patients and family with established coronary heart disease. The goal was to improve the outcomes of secondary prevention measures. The work was coordinated by the Cardiac Rehabilitation Centre, Udine, Italy, WHO Collaborating Centre for Research and Training in Rehabilitation and Secondary Prevention in Cardiovascular Diseases. The training was based on the principles of therapeutic patient education. The training sessions focused on basic knowledge of the structure and functioning of the cardiovascular system, guide symptoms and signs of emerging acute cardiovascular conditions, preventing and managing cardiovascular risk factors and principles of treatment. resume: This study aimed to examine the accuracy of death certificates for coding coronary heart disease [CHD] as the underlying cause of death in Bahrain. The coding of 459 death certificates [151 as CHD and 308 as other causes] by the Directorate of Public Health was similarly reviewed. The sensitivity and specificity of the hospital diagnosis were 76% and 72% respectively and those of the Directorate of Public Health were 85% and 89% respectively. titre: Framework for action on rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease in the WHO Eastern Mediterranean Region
resume: Globally rheumatic heart disease (RHD) is the leading cause of preventable cardiac death in people under the age of 25. RHD is caused by infection with Streptococcus A (Strep A) a widespread bacterium associated with infections that commonly occur in childhood. Untreated throat (and possibly skin) infection with Strep A (“strep throat”) triggers an autoimmune response in some children which then causes acute rheumatic fever (RF). RF affects the joints skin nervous system and heart. While patients with RF will typically recover the damage caused to the heart valves is permanent and can cause heart failure stroke heart rhythm problems and maternal death during pregnancy.Once a child is identified as having experienced RF regular antibiotic prophylaxis is required to prevent subsequent Strep A infections and consequent RF episodes which would further damage the heart.The vast majority of RF/RHD occurs in developing countries.It is a disease of poverty that is strongly associated with overcrowded living conditions.Available data indicate that RF/RHD presents a significant ongoing public health burden in the WHO Eastern Mediterranean Region. In May 2018 the World Health Assembly passed resolution WHA71.14 to prioritize action to address the global burden of RF/RHD. This regional framework for action on RF/RHD aims to guide implementation of this resolution in the Region.The framework was endorsed by Member States in resolution EM/RC66/R.1 of the WHO Regional Committee for the Eastern Mediterranean at the Committee’s 66th session in October 2019.

Key outcomes assessed include changes in knowledge, health service utilization and intervention effects across diverse populations. resume: This web annex provides detailed documentation of the processes, methods and key questions underpinning the development of WHO recommendations on the prevention and diagnosis of rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease. The document outlines the roles and contributions of the groups involved in the guideline development process, including the WHO Steering Group, the Guideline Development Group, systematic review teams and external reviewers, as well as processes for managing conflicts of interest and achieving consensus. It describes the use of structured approaches such as PICO frameworks, GRADE methods and evidence-to-decision frameworks to inform recommendations, and details the criteria used to determine their strength and direction. The annex also presents the full set of key clinical and public health questions that guided the evidence reviews. It is intended for researchers, methodologists, policy-makers and other stakeholders seeking to understand the methodological basis of the guideline.

resume: The Political Declaration of the High-level Meeting on Noncommunicable Diseases (NCDs) held in September 2011 in New York calls for concrete and comprehensive actions by Member States and the international community, and emphasizes WHO's leading role in coordinating global action against NCDs. As a follow-up of this meeting and as per the decision of the Sixty-fourth Session of the World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Committee for South-East Asia, a regional meeting was organized from 24 to 26 April in Yangon, Myanmar. It was a platform to facilitate discussions and consensus building on priority actions of the UN Political Declaration at regional and country levels. The regional meeting also facilitated Technical Discussions on Mental Health, including Mental and Neurological disorders. It provided a forum to discuss priority actions at regional and country levels to take the mental health agenda forward. The Technical Discussions also focused on alcohol as the common risk factor for NCDs and the substantial harm from alcohol use to an individual, the family and the community. The meeting was attended by 138 participants including 14 observers. The participants included representatives from all 11 Member States of the Region and from various agencies including the government, NGOs, WHO collaborating centres, academia and the UN. Based on the inputs received from Member States, a draft resolution on NCDs including mental health and neurological disorders was prepared. The recommendations arising out of the Technical Discussions will be submitted to the Sixty-fifth Session of the Regional Committee, to be held in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, from 5 to 7 September 2012.

titre: Strengthening primary care to address mental and neurological disorders
resume: WHO estimates that even though millions of people suffer from mental, neurological, behavioural or substance use disorders, only a fraction of these patients, particularly those in rural and remote areas, are getting appropriate medical care. Evidence for the limited outreach of the existing model of care for mental and neurological disorders is the huge treatment gap (defined as the percentage of patients in need of, but not receiving appropriate medical care), which ranges from 87 to 95% for patients with epilepsy and 25 to 98% for patients with psychosis, based on studies carried out in the Region. The WHO Regional Office for South-East Asia has therefore been working with regional experts on a strategy to improve access to appropriate care for persons with mental and neurological disorders. The strategy calls for empowering the existing primary health-care delivery systems in Member States to identify and manage the most common and disabling of these disorders. Such care can be provided at the doorstep of the patient, thus making it readily available, accessible and acceptable. This model has been tested in Bangladesh, Bhutan, Myanmar, Thailand and Timor-Leste and found to be very effective in reducing the treatment gap to a fraction of what it was.

titre: International travel and health: module 5: mental, neurological and substance use conditions
resume: International travel can influence mental, neurological and substance use (MNS) conditions through exposure to stress, disruption of routines and differences in health systems, legal frameworks and cultural contexts across destinations. This module provides technical guidance on the assessment and management of MNS-related risks in the context of travel, supporting health professionals in advising travellers with or at risk of such conditions. It examines general considerations, pre-travel assessment and continuity of care, including the safe use and transport of psychotropic medications and awareness of legal restrictions. The document describes a range of mental health conditions, such as anxiety disorders, depression, psychoses and stress-related conditions, as well as neurological disorders and emergencies, outlining potential triggers linked to travel and relevant preventive measures. It also addresses substance use and substance use disorders, including risks of intoxication, dependence, withdrawal and overdose in unfamiliar settings. Attention is given to variability in care infrastructure and its implications for access to services and potential repatriation, alongside a rights-based approach to care informed by WHO frameworks such as mhGAP and QualityRights. Particular consideration is given to vulnerable groups, including children, adolescents and individuals with chronic conditions, supporting continuity of care, social support and access to appropriate services.

It supports implementation of WHO global action plans related to mental health, epilepsy, dementia and alcohol use disorders. The guideline was developed in accordance with WHO standards for guideline development and uses systematic evidence reviews and the GRADE approach to formulate recommendations. It includes updated and new recommendations across 11 modules covering alcohol and drug use disorders, anxiety, depression, psychosis and bipolar disorder, epilepsy and seizures, dementia, stress-related conditions, self-harm and suicide, and child and adolescent mental disorders. The recommendations address pharmacological, psychological, psychosocial, digital and community-based interventions, while also considering feasibility, cost-effectiveness, human rights, sociocultural acceptability and equity. titre: Educating medical and nursing students to provide mental health, neurological and substance use care: a practical guide for pre-service education
resume: This practical guide provides evidence-informed recommendations to strengthen pre-service education for medical and nursing students in the delivery of mental health, neurological and substance use (MNS) care. It addresses the global burden of MNS conditions and the persistent treatment gap driven by limited access to quality services and shortages in the trained workforce. The document emphasizes the role of undergraduate education in equipping future health professionals with the competencies required to integrate MNS care into general health settings, in line with universal health coverage objectives . titre: Addressing mental and neurological disorders: Impact evaluation of ongoing projects to strengthen primary health-care : Report of the regional meeting of experts Dhaka, Bangladesh, -1-3 Dec 2011
resume: This regional meeting of experts on impact evaluation of the ongoing projects to strengthen the primary health-care system for mental health-care was convened by the WHO Regional Office for South-East Asia in collaboration with the WHO Country Office Bangladesh. Participants from eight SEAR Member States of the Region and five ASEAN countries attended the meeting. Recent developments in mental health have led to revised thinking about the delivery of care for mental and neurological disorders. One of the most important realizations has been that appropriate care for persons with mental and neurological disorders is best given in the community beyond the closed walls of psychiatric hospitals. This has lent a new dimension to approaches for care of patients with mental and neurological disorders. The strategy is to strengthen the existing primary health-care system with provision of essential medicines and with minimum investment in training. This strategy was piloted in Bangladesh, Bhutan, Thailand and Timor-Leste. The outcomes of the projects were assessed by measuring reduction in 'treatment gap'. The scope of the intervention to scale up the projects at national and cross-national levels were also evaluated in terms of acceptability and feasibility. The report details the impact of these projects and cites the challenges met, with recommendations for scaling up in countries where it has been piloted and for other countries to pilot these projects. This report will be ready reference for policy-makers and programme managers to develop country-specific projects for delivering care for mental and neurological disorders through the existing primary health-care system.

titre: Strengthening surveillance of and response to foodborne diseases: stage one manual (part B): investigating foodborne disease outbreaks
resume: This practical manual provides step-by-step guidance for investigating foodborne disease outbreaks, forming part of the first stage of WHO’s framework for strengthening surveillance and response systems. It is designed as an introductory, field-oriented resource to support rapid and effective outbreak investigation during acute public health events, particularly in countries developing their capacities. The manual is intended for public health practitioners, epidemiologists, laboratory personnel, food safety inspectors and other professionals involved in outbreak detection and response. The document outlines a structured, ten-step approach to outbreak investigation, organized into three phases: preparation before field deployment, field investigation, and post-investigation activities. It covers essential processes such as confirming the existence of an outbreak, defining and identifying cases, and describing the outbreak in terms of person, time and place, as well as generating and testing hypotheses through epidemiological, laboratory and environmental investigations. It also addresses trace-back activities, implementation of control measures and communication of findings. The manual emphasizes multidisciplinary collaboration and highlights that investigation steps may be iterative and adapted to local contexts. By providing practical tools and a clear operational framework, it supports early detection, effective control and prevention of foodborne disease outbreaks.

titre: Key advocacy messages for chronic respiratory diseases
resume: Chronic respiratory diseases represent a major yet under-recognized component of the global noncommunicable disease burden, affecting nearly 500 million people and causing approximately 4 million deaths each year, with disproportionate impacts in low- and middle-income countries. This advocacy-oriented document presents key messages developed by the Global Alliance against Chronic Respiratory Diseases to elevate the priority of conditions such as asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease within global and national health agendas, particularly in the context of the 2025 United Nations High-Level Meeting on noncommunicable diseases. The publication outlines the scale, determinants and consequences of chronic respiratory diseases, emphasizing that they are preventable and manageable but remain insufficiently integrated into noncommunicable disease policy frameworks. It identifies priority actions for Member States, including integrating these conditions into national strategies and universal health coverage commitments, addressing major risk factors such as tobacco use, air pollution and occupational exposures through multisectoral policies, and strengthening primary health care systems to improve diagnosis, long-term management and access to essential medicines and technologies. The document also highlights the need for investment in data systems and research to support evidence-informed policy-making. Intended for policy-makers and stakeholders, it provides a concise advocacy framework aligned with Sustainable Development Goals 3.4 and 3.8 to guide coordinated action and reduce the global burden of chronic respiratory diseases.

titre: Chronic respiratory diseases in the WHO European Region
resume: This report on chronic respiratory diseases (CRDs) in the WHO European Region, developed by WHO and the European Respiratory Society (ERS), highlights that despite progress in reducing CRD mortality, their burden and related inequities remain high. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and asthma are the most prevalent CRDs, with nearly 80% of CRD deaths caused by COPD.With an ageing population and multiple intertwined crises, COPD cases are projected to increase by 23% globally by 2050, with woman and those living in low- and middle-income countries more greatly affected. Regional productivity loss between 30 and 74 years due to CRDs is estimated at US$20.7 billion. With the Region, disparities are evident, with high CRD prevalence in the western part, but high hospitalization and mortality rates in the eastern part. This report emphasizes the need for integrated health system responses and prioritization of resources to address these disparities and advance CRD surveillance, research and innovation agendas. It provides a set of essential interventions, policy options and country examples, emphasizing the importance of tobacco and air quality control, addressing social determinants of health and ensuring continuum of care. By leveraging this report, countries can prioritize essential CRD interventions, enhance their health systems, reduce inequities and improve the quality of life for those living with CRDs.

titre: Global scientific panel on chronic respiratory diseases: background paper
resume: Chronic respiratory diseases represent a substantial and often under-recognized component of the global noncommunicable disease burden, affecting hundreds of millions of people and contributing significantly to premature mortality and disability. Developed in the context of the 2025 United Nations High-Level Meeting on noncommunicable diseases, this document presents a background paper prepared by the Global Alliance against Chronic Respiratory Diseases (GARD) to inform the work of a global scientific panel, synthesizing evidence from the scientific literature and country experiences to support policy dialogue. It examines the epidemiology and determinants of asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, emphasizing their disproportionate impact in low- and middle-income countries and among vulnerable populations. The paper outlines five priority areas for action: elevating the profile of chronic respiratory diseases within national and global agendas; fostering multisectoral partnerships to address environmental and behavioural risk factors; strengthening primary health care to support prevention, diagnosis and long-term management; ensuring equitable access to essential medicines and technologies; and investing in research, surveillance and data systems to inform policy. Intended for policy-makers, health authorities and partners, it provides a structured evidence base to support integrated, equitable and scalable responses aligned with universal health coverage and sustainable development goals.

titre: Chronic respiratory diseases in children in relation to air pollution: report on a WHO study
resume: A considerable amount of research has been conducted over the past 20 years into the possible hazards to health from air pollution, particularly where exposure may have lasted for many years. Research has been directed mainly towards defining the relationship between exposure to air pollution and the development of respiratory disorders. The results of those studies had been sufficiently encouraging for the WHO Regional Office for Europe to consider organizing an international collaborative study on the relationship between air pollution and respiratory disease in children. The background to this action was a Working Group, convened by the Regional Office in Copenhagen in January 1971, which drew up a long-term programme on environmental pollution control in Europe. The Working Group concluded that studies carried out among children would be the most promising field of research on the medical effects of air pollution. The Regional Office subsequently convened a Working Group in Copenhagen in February 1972 which reviewed studies on the relationship between air pollution and respiratory disease in children that had so far been carried out in the European Region. The Working Group agreed that new studies should be conducted within the framework of the long-term programme on environmental pollution control. Using information from the earlier studies, the Working Group prepared an outline for a coordinated study of air pollution and its possible effects on respiratory disease in children.

titre: Burden of acute respiratory disease of epidemic and pandemic potential in the WHO Eastern Mediterranean Region: a literature review
resume: There are gaps in the knowledge about the burden of severe respiratory disease in the Eastern Mediterranean Region [EMR]. This literature review was therefore conducted to describe the burden of epidemic- and pandemic-prone acute respiratory infections [ARI] in the Region which may help in the development of evidence-based disease prevention and control policies. Relevant published and unpublished reports were identified from searches of various databases; 83 documents fulfilled the search criteria. The infections identified included: ARI, avian influenza A[H5N1], influenza A[H1N1]pdm09 and Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus [MERS-CoV] infection. Pneumonia and ARIs were leading causes of disease and death in the Region. Influenza A[H1N1] was an important cause of morbidity during the 2009 pandemic. This review provides a descriptive summary of the burden of acute respiratory diseases in the Region, but there still remains a lack of necessary data

titre: Report of the eighteenth annual meeting of the Global Alliance against Chronic Respiratory Diseases: virtual meeting, 28 October 2025
resume: Coordinated global action is essential to reduce the growing burden of chronic respiratory diseases (CRDs), particularly in low- and middle-income countries where access to prevention, diagnosis and care remains uneven. This report summarizes the proceedings of the eighteenth annual meeting of the Global Alliance against Chronic Respiratory Diseases (GARD), held virtually on 28 October 2025. It documents key discussions, strategic priorities and collaborative efforts aimed at advancing integrated approaches to lung health within the broader noncommunicable disease (NCD) agenda, while serving as a platform for knowledge exchange and coordination among stakeholders. The report is intended for policymakers, public health authorities, partner organizations and stakeholders engaged in respiratory health and health system strengthening. The report is structured around three main areas: high-level global commitments on CRDs, including updates on the World Health Assembly resolution on lung health and the United Nations high-level meeting on NCDs; actions to improve prevention and care, such as expanding access to inhaled medicines, strengthening primary care and advancing implementation research; and GARD governance and collaboration mechanisms. It highlights priority themes including air pollution, equitable access to treatment, primary care strengthening and patient engagement, and underscores the need to translate global commitments into concrete national action. By capturing key achievements, challenges and opportunities, the report supports continued collaboration and informed action to reduce the global burden of CRDs.

The meeting brought together representatives from WHO, GARD member organizations and partner institutions to review progress in addressing chronic respiratory diseases (CRDs), particularly asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), with a focus on low- and middle-income countries. The report outlines developments in GARD governance, membership and communications, including expansion of the alliance network and progress in the WHO Knowledge Action Portal on noncommunicable diseases. The publication also presents updates from WHO on CRD-related activities, including tobacco cessation resources, public awareness initiatives, and planned updates to global guidelines for asthma and COPD management in primary care. Discussions highlighted the appointment of the WHO Director-General’s Special Envoy for CRDs, preparations for major global health events in 2025, and collaborative efforts to improve equitable access to inhaled medicines and strengthen CRD care. Case studies and discussions emphasized the importance of political commitment, integrated primary health care approaches, patient engagement and international collaboration to reduce the global burden of chronic respiratory diseases.

titre: Prevalence of visual impairment and eye diseases in Afghan refugees in Pakistan
resume: The prevalence and etiology of visual loss and eye diseases were determined in a resident Afghan refugee community in northern Pakistan. The survey included 1156 people and revealed that 2.1% of the population were blind and 6.9% were visually impaired according to WHO criteria. The leading causes of blindness included cataract [62.5%], uncorrected refractive errors [16.6%], retinal degeneration/dystrophy [12.5%], glaucoma [4.2%] and microphthalmos [4.2%]. The causes of visual loss were uncorrected refractive errors [46.2%], cataract [32.7%] and corneal opacities [4.8%]. These conditions were also important causes of unilateral lost vision. Active trachoma was found in 3.7% of all children under 10 years of age

titre: Eye care indicator menu (ECIM): a tool for monitoring strategies and actions for eye care provision
resume: he Eye Care Indicator Menu (ECIM) is a World Health Organization tool designed to support countries in monitoring strategies and actions for eye care provision within the framework of integrated people-centred eye care and universal health coverage. The publication presents a standardized set of indicators intended to strengthen the integration of eye care into national health information systems and to support the development, implementation and evaluation of eye care monitoring frameworks at national and subnational levels. It outlines the rationale, structure and intended use of the ECIM, including its alignment with the recommendations of the World report on vision and World Health Assembly resolution WHA73.4. The document describes 13 core indicators and 13 expanded indicators covering governance, financing, workforce, information systems, service access and quality, coverage, and impact. For each indicator, detailed metadata are provided, including definitions, methods of measurement, disaggregation dimensions, frequency of measurement and preferred data sources. The ECIM is intended to assist policy-makers, planners and health information system managers in improving the availability, comparability and use of eye care data to guide planning, resource allocation and evaluation of eye care services.

titre: Vision and eye screening implementation handbook
resume: This handbook provides practical guidance for planning and implementing vision and eye screening programmes at community and primary health care levels, with a focus on high-risk population groups across the life course. Developed by WHO as a companion to the Package of eye care interventions, it supports the integration of evidence-based, cost–effective screening strategies into health systems, particularly in low- and low–intermediate-resource settings. The document is intended for policy-makers, programme managers and service providers responsible for organizing and delivering eye care services. The handbook outlines minimum recommendations for screening during the neonatal period, in pre-school and school-aged children, and among older adults. It describes screening protocols, required human resources, equipment and infrastructure, referral pathways, and follow-up mechanisms within the continuum of care. In addition, it addresses service delivery approaches, including refractive error services and the use of telehealth, and highlights the importance of health promotion, community engagement, and monitoring and evaluation. By promoting early detection and timely intervention, the publication aims to improve access to appropriate care, reduce preventable vision impairment, and strengthen equitable and sustainable eye care services.

titre: Eliminate yellow fever epidemics (EYE) strategy country toolkit
resume: This country toolkit provides practical, ready-to-use guidance to support the implementation of activities under the Eliminate Yellow fever Epidemics (EYE) Strategy, with the aim of preventing and controlling yellow fever outbreaks. It consolidates technical expertise and operational insights from multiple global partners to inform country-level action across the full spectrum of prevention, detection and response. The toolkit is designed for public health professionals, surveillance officers and immunization programme managers involved in yellow fever control. It offers structured guidance to strengthen population immunity through routine immunization and preventive mass vaccination campaigns, improve case detection and investigation, and support timely and effective outbreak response, including measures to prevent international spread. Organized into thematic modules, the document covers key areas such as risk assessment, vaccination strategies, surveillance and laboratory capacity, communication and community engagement, campaign planning and monitoring, and access to vaccine stockpiles. It also emphasizes the importance of reaching vulnerable and at-risk populations, strengthening coordination and governance, and integrating activities with broader health system and immunization programmes. Overall, the toolkit aims to support countries in implementing coordinated, evidence-based and context-specific interventions to reduce the risk of yellow fever epidemics and strengthen global health security.

titre: Oman Eye Study 2005: prevalence and determinants of glaucoma
resume: This community-based study was carried out to estimate the prevalence and identify the determinants of glaucoma in the Omani population in 2005-06. Residents of 75 randomly selected houses in 25 clusters participated in the survey. We interviewed and examined 3324 individuals aged >/= 30 years in their homes and in eye clinics to note personal details, glaucoma status and presence of selected risk factors: 180 were diagnosed as having glaucoma. Projected prevalence of glaucoma among the Omani population >/= 30 years was 4.75%. Open angle and angle closure types of glaucoma contributed 40.6% and 37.8% respectively. History of hypertension was negatively, and older age and family history of glaucoma were positively, associated with glaucoma

titre: Causes of low vision and blindness in a Turkish adult population: the Izmir eye study
resume: Background: Data from Turkey show that sense organ diseases were the second leading cause of years lost due to disability in 2015. However, there are no reliable data on either the baseline causative disorders of visual impairment or the burden of these disorders on the population in Izmir region. Izmir is the third most populated city of Turkey with a population of approximately 4.2 million. Aim: The purpose of this study was to define the baseline disorders causing low vision and blindness in accordance with World Health Organization criteria in an adult population in Izmir. Methods: We evaluated the ophthalmologic reports of 20 790 people in Izmir, Turkey. Age- and sex-specific causes of low vision and blindness were identified. Results: Bilateral low vision and blindness was detected in 347 people, 172 males and 175 females. For those aged 18–50 years, retinal dystrophies [37%], congenital eye anomalies [14%] and myopic degenerations [13%] were the most common causes. For those aged 50+ years, age-related macular degeneration [21%] was the leading cause. Diabetic retinopathy [17%], corneal opacities [14%], cataract [12%] and glaucoma [9%] were also important. Sex was not a significant determinant. Conclusion: The specific causes of visual impairment vary greatly with age, however, unavoidable retinal pathologies were the predominant causes at all ages

titre: Oman Eye Study 2005: validity of screening tests used in the glaucoma survey
resume: We carried out a validity assessment study for glaucoma screening procedures used during the survey conducted in Oman in 2005 on 6644 eyes in 3324 people >/= 30 years. Ocular pressure and fundus changes were the screening parameters used: glaucoma was found in 433 eyes. Sensitivity for ocular pressure was 49.7% and specificity 95.6%. For optic disc changes, sensitivity was 48.4% and specificity 97.9%. Combining both through parallel testing, sensitivity improved to 67.3% and specificity to 96.5%. An eye may, thus, be declared as not having glaucoma, but cannot be labelled as having glaucoma, using these parameters

titre: Framework for implementing the global strategy to eliminate yellow fever epidemics (EYE), 2017–2026 in the African Region: report of the Secretariat
resume: 1. Despite the availability of a vaccine with life-long immunity, the majority of countries in the World Health Organization African Region are at risk of yellow fever (YF). This is because the national immunization coverage for YF is not yet optimal.2. To respond to frequent YF outbreaks in West Africa, the YF Initiative (YFI) has, since 2005, supported efforts to reduce the burden of this disease. Although surveillance and response capacities have been progressively improved, over 440 million people remain at risk of YF in the African Region. The recent yellow fever outbreak in Angola and DRC clearly demonstrated that this disease is still a serious health risk within and outside the Region.3. Currently, the Region is challenged by suboptimal routine YF vaccination, frequent vaccine stock-outs and inadequate implementation of the International Health Regulations (IHR 2005). Further, other risk factors such as climate change and rapid urbanization lead to frequent YF outbreaks.4. In view of the foregoing, a global strategy to eliminate yellow fever epidemics (EYE) for the period 2017–2026 was developed in 2016. This regional implementation framework has been developed to support the rollout of the global strategy. The three strategic objectives are: (i) to protect populations in all 35 countries at risk through preventive and routine vaccination; (ii) to prevent the international spread of YF through vaccination of travellers and robust screening at major points of entry; and (iii) to detect, confirm and rapidly contain YF outbreaks.5. The framework also clearly stipulates the targets and milestones. With a single dose of YF vaccine per person, elimination of YF epidemics is indeed a quick public health gain. The Regional Committee is invited to examine and adopt the actions proposed in this framework.

titre: Better noncommunicable disease outcomes: challenges and opportunities for health systems: Tajikistan country assessment: focus on cardiovascular disease
resume: Cardiovascular diseases are the predominant cause of death in Tajikistan, with a growing burden of ischaemic heart disease, strokes and cirrhosis between 1990 and 2010. Considering this, this report focuses on cardiovascular diseases and their risk factors, such as hypertension and poor nutrition; it is estimated that 40% of the Tajik population is overweight and 9% is obese. Other risk factors such as diabetes and tobacco use are also analysed. While Tajikistan has made some progress in implementing anti-smoking policies and reducing the harmful use of alcohol, opportunities such as better enforcement and monitoring of legislation exist. Significant challenges also remain for coverage of core individual services, especially in the effective diagnosis and management of key cardiovascular disease conditions, such as hypertension and diabetes. This report identifies key health system challenges that prevent greater coverage of core noncommunicable diseases interventions and services, and proposes three strategic recommendations to accelerate gains in cardiovascular diseases outcomes.

titre: Operational manual on indoor residual spraying: control of vectors of malaria, Aedes-borne diseases, Chagas disease, leishmaniases and lymphatic filariasis
resume: Indoor residual spraying is a key vector control intervention for preventing and controlling a range of vector-borne diseases by targeting insects that rest on interior surfaces of dwellings. This operational manual provides comprehensive, updated technical guidance on the design, implementation and evaluation of indoor residual spraying programmes for malaria, Aedes-borne diseases, Chagas disease, leishmaniases and lymphatic filariasis. It reflects current WHO recommendations and aligns with the Global vector control response, expanding previous malaria-focused guidance to address multiple diseases and programmatic contexts. The intervention is presented as a community-level strategy requiring high coverage to reduce vector density and interrupt transmission, particularly for endophilic and endophagic vectors. It is intended to support national and subnational programme managers, technical staff and implementing partners responsible for planning and delivering vector control interventions. The document outlines key components of effective programmes, including policy development, planning, resource mobilization, training and community engagement, alongside detailed operational procedures for spray campaigns. It covers insecticide selection, procurement and resistance management, supply chain and logistics, occupational and environmental safety, supervision and quality assurance, and monitoring and evaluation. Structured around the full programme cycle—from preparation through implementation to review—it provides standardized tools, indicators and practical guidance to support high-quality, safe and effective spraying operations. The manual also emphasizes adaptation to local epidemiological and entomological conditions and strengthening system capacity to ensure sustained and effective vector control.

titre: Annual report 2002: division of communicable disease control
resume: Communicable diseases are responsible for the deaths of an estimated 1.3 million people in the Eastern Mediterranean Region every year. Most of these deaths could have been prevented with proper utilization of the available cost effective prevention and control measures. Unfortunately, this is not the case, and millions still die of communicable diseases every year. To address this situation, the Regional Office has promoted the concept of integrated disease control, in which better use of available resources and wider coverage of intervention techniques will lead to improve health for the people of the Region. The Annual Report 2002 of the Division of Communicable Disease Control is a transparent look at the difficulties we must overcome and the challenges we face in doing so. It is a pragmatic analysis of the magnitude of the problems we are attempting to resolve and the complexities inherent in implementing a new approach in an ever-changing environment.The DCD Annual Report 2001 focuses on the situation of communicable diseases in the Eastern Mediterranean Region. It looks extensively at the disease burden in general and specific diseases in particular. it discusses general prevention and control measures, with examples of successes and pitfalls. Finally, it proposed a new approach, the 'integrated approach', to scale up control activities and develop an essential package of services that can be delivered at the periphery under whatever conditions

titre: Healthy nutrition: preventing nutrition-related diseases in Europe
resume: What do Europeans eat? How does their diet affect their health? How and what kind of changes in diet could protect or improve their health? This book provides answers to these questions, acting on the wealth of evidence linking diet to disease and on the call of European expert committees for public health policies to ensure that people in Europe can choose a healthy diet. All Member States in the Region have food policies, but nutrition policies are needed for clear health objectives. The authors are medical nutritionists and they fill this need by presenting a set of nutrient goals, based on national recommendations and reflecting an ideal nutritional pattern for the prevention of noncommunicable diseases. Policy-makers can use these goals to build nutrition policies that meet their particular needs. The authors’ aim is to help countries to improve health by building their own coherent food and nutrition policies. Such policies should take account not only of prevention but also of national dietary and cultural traditions, and the economic and other problems involved in changing the provision of food. This book should be a catalyst; it can both aid and challenge policy-makers, health professionals, nutritionists, people in the food and agricultural industries and the general public. Each of these groups has an important role in the broad intersectoral action needed to make a success of food policies that take account of health. Through such action and such policies, people in Europe can achieve the balanced nutrition that is so necessary a part of health for all.
